evidence.quote: EFS provides close-to-open consistency: after a writer finishes writing and successfully closes, a later opener can see the changes. This is not a promise that an already-open reader immediately sees every concurrent write. Follow the client and service's documented cache rules.

EFS documents storage across Availability Zones for Regional filesystem writes at successful synchronous completion, such as fsync, or file close. An Availability Zone is an isolated infrastructure location within a cloud Region. This durability boundary does not make several writes a transaction or protect them from later deletion.

EFS locks are advisory: a program that ignores the lock can still read or write. All participants must cooperate with the same supported locking protocol. Sharing a directory alone does not provide that cooperation.

Check the actual failure boundary. EFS Regional stores data across multiple Availability Zones; EFS One Zone stores it within one zone and can lose data in a zone disaster. The generic file-storage interface does not imply either placement.

mechanisms.reason: The file-interface objective identifies named bytes, directory paths, metadata and service ownership. Mounting traces program, OS client, cache/network and service; its diagram is attached to displayed card 2 because the component receives a zero-based index. Caches/completion separates volatile pending state, visibility and durable completion. Coordination shows the actual 10-to-11 lost update and full lock scope, with the matching card-4 diagram showing two writes producing 11. Identity checks, outage retries, inconsistent live backups and operation overhead each provide a causal explanation rather than terminology alone.

evidence.quote: The program calls the operating system. Its filesystem client sends needed requests across the network to the file service and returns results to the program. Some requests can use a client cache, a local copy kept to avoid another network trip.

A client can cache file contents and metadata, and buffer pending writes in volatile memory. An ordinary buffered write can succeed before its bytes reach the service. A client crash can lose those bytes; remote persistent storage cannot preserve data it never received.

Suppose two clients each read a counter of 10, compute 11 and write 11. Both file writes can succeed, yet the final value is 11 rather than 12. The filesystem performed the individual operations; it did not make each read-compute-write sequence one indivisible update.

A live file backup is not automatically an atomic application snapshot. AWS warns that writes, renames, moves or deletes during an EFS backup can leave inconsistent results. Related files may reflect different stages of an application update.

coherence.reason: All nine objectives are taught in dependency order: file vocabulary precedes paths and caches; completion precedes concurrent updates; identity follows mounting; outage scope builds on durability; backup builds on partial updates and failure; performance reuses operation and locking costs; fit consolidates those responsibilities. The two diagrams clarify the corresponding mechanisms without implying extra guarantees. A recurring story is not necessary for these connected explanations.

evidence.quote: A file holds bytes under a name. Directories organize those names into paths, such as /assets/logo.svg. Metadata describes a file: its size, owner and access permissions. A shared file service maintains this filesystem and accepts file operations from multiple hosts.

Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a directory in a host's local path tree. After mounting a share at /shared, a program can open /shared/report.csv using its usual file operations. This does not copy the dataset to the host or require formatting a client disk.

A single writer can process updates in order. Alternatively, every participant can use a supported lock, a coordination rule that reserves access while an update runs. Acquire it before reading, protect the entire read-modify-write sequence and release it after completing the required writes. Locking only the final write leaves the stale-read problem.

A managed file service can remove file-server administration. Application coordination, identities and permissions, network access, workload performance and tested recovery still need deliberate choices. Match those responsibilities to the workload before selecting the service.

decisions.reason: Each practical objective includes consequences and a choice: cooperate over an entire update or use a single writer; retain transaction recovery for multi-file changes; diagnose IDs and permission layers rather than opening all access; accept hard-mount waiting while planning outages; retain usable history and test restores; measure overhead and lock contention before buying performance; choose storage by interface and verify database compatibility. Benefits and limits are tied to mechanisms and support transfer to another workload.

evidence.quote: Align the intended identities and grant only the access the application needs. Making the whole share writable by everyone hides the diagnosis and grants unrelated clients permission to damage data.

With an NFS hard mount, timed-out requests keep retrying until the server responds. Application I/O can wait during an outage. Switching to soft timeouts is not a harmless responsiveness fix: returned errors and interrupted operations can introduce data-integrity risks. Follow supported mount settings and design how the application handles unavailable storage.

Restore a suitable recovery point to a controlled destination. Check files, permissions and application behavior, and measure the recovery time. Choose backup frequency and retention around how much work you can afford to lose and how long you can be down. A successful backup job alone does not prove a usable restore.

Measure a representative workload: operation sizes and mix, metadata activity, latency, aggregate throughput and lock waits. Check client, network and service limits before increasing provisioned performance or parallelism. Change the part that limits the workload rather than assuming more storage or more hosts will help.

A database may keep its own files on shared storage only when it supports the chosen filesystem's locking, durability and recovery behavior. Several database processes pointed at one directory do not automatically form a safe multi-writer database. Check the engine's requirements before choosing that layout.

evidence.quote: Ask when the service has safely stored the bytes. Use the supported completion procedure, including sending application-held buffers onward, awaiting the required flush or close and checking errors. fsync is a file synchronization operation; it cannot send bytes still held only in an application's private buffer.

A lock also cannot undo half an update after a crash. When several related files must change together, use an application or database transaction and recovery design. Atomic recovery means related changes can be recovered as a complete update rather than an arbitrary subset.

EFS uses Unix-style ownership and permissions with numeric user IDs and group IDs. Read permission allows reading file contents; write permission allows modifying them. A directory's execute, or search, permission allows traversal through that directory to a path beneath it.

Capacity measures stored bytes. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Latency is the time one operation takes. Increasing capacity does not by itself promise faster access.

sourceChecks.claim: Checked file hierarchy, metadata, shared operations and addressed block/object interfaces. Database transactions are corroborated by the PostgreSQL followup, not this comparison page alone.

Mount targets provide network access to the EFS filesystem; security groups and NFS permissions remain relevant. Generic mount and cache mechanics additionally checked in nfs(5). Primary followup https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html: Mount attaches the remote filesystem to the local namespace; NFS provides file sharing over a network. It is not filesystem formatting or dataset duplication.

EFS explicitly documents close-to-open and Regional durable writes at synchronous operation or close. This is a scoped service promise; stronger guarantees are not inferred. Primary followup https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html: Close-to-open writes pending data on close for later openers; caching may be stale during concurrent work. Buffered writes can wait on the client; documented locking is needed for coherent coordinated access. Primary followup https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/fflush.3.html: fflush transfers user-space library buffers; kernel buffers require a separate synchronization step. This substantiates the lesson warning about application-held bytes. Primary followup https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html: fsync synchronizes modified kernel file state and reports completion/errors; it does not consume private application buffers or promise multi-file atomicity.

EFS supports NFSv4 locks but read/write operations do not check conflicting advisory locks. Serialization and multi-step recovery are separately corroborated. Primary followup https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html: Multi-step all-or-nothing database behavior requires transactions; individual filesystem writes and cooperative locks are not that recovery mechanism.

EFS checks numeric ownership/user/group IDs rather than names; different IDs yield different users. Permissions still apply after mounting. Primary followup https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/iam-access-control-nfs-efs.html: ClientMount and ClientWrite are distinct authorization actions; IAM client authorization is configurable and separate from Unix file identity. Primary followup https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/user-and-group-permissions.html: EFS uses standard Unix read/write/execute permissions based on numeric identities, including configured access-point overrides; the lesson appropriately asks for effective identities. Primary followup https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/path_resolution.7.html: Search permission is required while traversing directory components; directory execute is search, unlike ordinary-file execution.

Hard requests retry indefinitely; AWS recommends hard mounting for integrity and warns soft mounts risk corruption. Placement is verified in the EFS features source, not inferred from mount settings. Primary followup https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/features.html: Regional spans zones; One Zone data can be lost in an AZ disaster. No implication that redundant storage protects against client failure or later authorized modification. Primary followup https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-regions-availability-zones.html: AWS defines Availability Zones as isolated locations within a Region.

Scheduling/retention and restore destinations are documented. Writes, rename, move and delete during backup can produce inconsistencies; AWS recommends pausing modifications or an unmodified period. Restore validation is an application-level recommendation, not an AWS guarantee.
Per-operation overhead, open/close round trips, larger-I/O amortization and contention-minimizing parallelism support the workload explanation. Pending asynchronous writes can remain on the client.

PostgreSQL permits NFS subject to required hard mounting and durable fsync/export behavior; it assumes supported filesystem semantics and describes a cluster managed by one server instance. This supports checking each engine, not a blanket prohibition on databases on NFS.
